claims.claim: Chicago-style steppin' is a partner dance that evolved from the Chicago Bop of the late 1940s–1960s, which itself derived from East Coast swing dances (Jitterbug, Lindy Hop).
claims.evidence: Multiple independent accounts converge: community-held history distinguishes Bopping (parents of Baby Boomers, swing family, smoothed in Chicago) from the youth New Bop of the early 1970s; TRiiBE locates origins on South/West Sides in the 1940s–50s; Emory/Atlanta Studies describes it as a partnered ballroom-style swing-family dance.
claims.notes: Distilled from MUSIC-001 gap note #6 (dance communities archived as footnotes).
claims.source: pancocojams.blogspot.com (quoting Society of Boppers, Steppers & Walkers, profmilesproduction.com); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_stepping; TRiiBE (2026-09); Emory News/Atlanta Studies (Anjulet Tucker)
claims.source_type: specialist secondary / tertiary / local journalism / institutional

claims.claim: No published syllabus exists for Chicago-style steppin'; transmission is oral, visual, and generational ('watch and learn').
claims.evidence: Sustained absence-of-record corroborated by community sources describing transmission via parents, family members, and watching footwork.
claims.notes: MUSIC-001 flagged this as its dance-community gap; this brief treats the oral-transmission model as a finding, not a deficit.
claims.source: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 research-brief.md; en.wikipedia.org (citing archived practitioner page); TRiiBE (2026-09) quoting Valerie Hill ('family lineage and heritage handed down'); pancocojams (Society of Boppers page: 'watch and learn generation'); Mary Harris practitioner account
claims.source_type: sibling research / tertiary / local journalism / practitioner

claims.claim: DJ Sam Chatman ('Godfather of Steppin'') is widely credited with coining the name 'steppin'' for the dance.
claims.evidence: Independent attribution across local TV, Black press, and community histories. Account: Chatman saw a couple separate on the floor, took the mic and said it looked like they were 'stepping'/'step on'; he then printed the phrase on posters and flyers.
claims.notes: The attribution is consistent; the DATE of the coining is disputed (see C004). The story itself is practitioner oral history — treat as community-held origin narrative.
claims.source: WLS-TV/ABC7 Chicago 'Windy City LIVE' (2020-01-15); WLS-TV (2022-02-09, Samantha Chatman reporting); N'DIGO (2025-08-25); Bronzeville Winery event page (2023); TRiiBE (2026-09); Society of Boppers page
claims.source_type: local TV journalism / Black press / local journalism / practitioner community

claims.claim: Sam Chatman coined 'steppin'' in 1974.
claims.contradictory_evidence: TRiiBE (2026-09): 'In the 1960s, the term "steppin'" was officially coined by renowned Chicago DJ Sam Chatman.'
claims.evidence: Wikipedia's 1974 date rests on a single citation (WLS-TV 2022 segment). Community-held history places the transition in the mid-1970s.
claims.notes: Two published sources place the coining in different decades. No primary document (flyer, recording) has surfaced in this research pass.
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_stepping (citing WLS-TV 2022); Society of Boppers page (mid-1970s; 'New Bop' 1972–75)

claims.claim: 'Chicago is the steppin' capital of the world' is a phrase coined by Sam Chatman.
claims.evidence: Single-sourced attribution; the phrase is in wide community circulation.
claims.notes: Keep as PROVISIONAL until a Chatman interview transcript confirms it.
claims.source: YouTube: 'The History of the Chicago Dance Style Known as Steppin' From the 1940s to Today' (description); repeated in community usage

claims.claim: The 'New Bop' youth variation emerged around 1971–75 with music fueled by the J.B.'s ('Gimme Some More', 'Pass the Peas'), shifting the dance from one hand to two hands and front-to-back to side-to-side motion.
claims.evidence: Two sources converge on the J.B.'s → New Bop mechanism; both draw on community memory rather than archival records.
claims.notes: Release year of 'Gimme Some More' (1971) is itself a discographic claim not independently verified here — the dance-historical portion is what is graded.
claims.source: Society of Boppers page (via pancocojams); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_stepping

claims.claim: Jeffree's 'Love's Gonna Last' is the steppers' national anthem — a local (non-charting) record made into a classic by the Chicago stepper scene.
claims.evidence: AllMusic: Jeffree Perry (brother of Invictus/Hot Wax songwriter Greg Perry) recorded 'Love's Gonna Last' which 'became known as the steppers national anthem.' RadioInsight: Jeffree's 'Love's Gonna Last' was a 1978 MCA album track yielding only one minor chart single, but 'Chicago's stepper scene made it a local anthem.' Community accounts describe massive requests and WBMX play making it 'the ultimate Chicago-style steppers cut.'
claims.notes: 'National anthem' is community honorific, not an institutional designation. The mechanism — a dance community making a record a (local) hit — is the analytical point.
claims.source: AllMusic (Ed Hogan, Greg Perry biography); RadioInsight (Sean Ross, trade press); yolosteppers.com; ourdjtalk.com community thread

claims.claim: R. Kelly's 'Step in the Name of Love' (2003, Chocolate Factory) described Chicago stepping, became an impromptu steppers anthem, and carried the dance into national mainstream culture; the remix reached #1 on the Billboard R&B/Hip-Hop chart and #9 on the Hot 100.
claims.evidence: Chart data (10th R&B #1 for Kelly; Hot 100 peak #9, Dec 2 2003; UK double A-side with 'Thoia Thoing'). Wikipedia: original describes 'a dance style initially created in Chicago called stepping'; follow-up album Happy People/U Saved Me (2004) disc one heavily featured the dance/music. Practitioner: 'R. Kelly truly revived the form with his 2003 song.'
claims.notes: Handle with care: Kelly is a convicted sex offender. This brief records only the song's documented cultural function. Alchetron/community claim that R. Kelly's promotion gains were later 'dissolved' by poor community teaching/promotion is single-source and excluded from findings.
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Step_in_the_Name_of_Love; theaudiodb.com track record; LSU Reveille (practitioner instructor Christopher Jarrell)

claims.claim: The 1997 film Love Jones features Chicago stepping / a steppers-ball scene, bringing the culture to the big screen.
claims.evidence: Community sources consistently cite the film. The film object itself (1997, New Line Cinema) is independently verifiable as a Chicago-set romance.
claims.notes: Kept at PROVISIONAL pending verification of the specific scene by a citable source; the film's existence and Chicago setting are not in doubt.
claims.source: yolosteppers.com; ourdjtalk.com community thread

claims.claim: The 35th Annual World's Largest Steppers Competition took place on 2026-09-19 at the Tinley Park Convention Center (18501 S. Harlem Ave), with four categories (beginners, old school, ages 60-plus, new school), $10,000 in cash prizes, and finalists from prelims in Atlanta, Detroit, Houston, Los Angeles and New York City.
claims.evidence: Two TRiiBE reports: preview (event announced) and post-event photo gallery naming 2026 winners (Krystal Holmes & Ryan Robinson, beginners; Jerry McNair & Chessie Smith, 60 & Over). Attendance expectation ~3,500 (host Stephen 'Snoopy' King).
claims.notes: 'World's Largest' is the event's own title — a superlative that should be attributed, not asserted as fact.
claims.source: The TRiiBE (2026-09, two articles: preview and photo gallery)

claims.claim: For decades the World's Largest Steppers Competition was hosted and produced by Chicago steppin' legend Pete Frazier and his organization Majestic Gents; in 2026 he passed the torch to former champion and master instructor Stephen 'Snoopy' King.
claims.evidence: TRiiBE: 'For decades, the competition has always been hosted and produced by Chicago steppin' legend, Mr. Pete Frazier, and his steppin' organization, Majestic Gents.' King: member of Majestic Gents for 14 years, leader of Snoop & Crew.
claims.notes: Practitioner interview: 'Rodney Burke' is named as founder of the WLSC in a YouTube interview title (see C012) — hosting/producing by Frazier and founding by Burke are compatible.
claims.source: The TRiiBE (2026-09), quoting King and media rep Valerie Hill

claims.claim: Rodney Burke founded the World's Largest Steppers Contest.
claims.evidence: Title-level claim only; interview content not reviewed in this pass.
claims.notes: Founder vs. longtime producer distinction unresolved. Do not assert in public copy until the interview is reviewed or a second source confirms.
claims.source: YouTube interview: 'An interview with The Founder of The Worlds Largest Steppers Contest, Mr Rodney Burke'

claims.claim: The competition began 'over 35 years ago in local social and dance clubs' (implying an origin circa 1991 for a 2026 35th annual); footage exists from the 1994 contest (Pete Frazier and Darlinda Russell) and 2001 contest (Tyk Myn & Angie Faine; Bow Legs & Rhonda Freeman; Steppin B and Lenora).
claims.evidence: '35th Annual' in 2026 → arithmetic origin ~1991/1992; TRiiBE: 'began over 35 years ago.' Archival footage dates are uploader-asserted.
claims.notes: The exact founding year is not established in a citable source — grade the arithmetic as PROVISIONAL.
claims.source: The TRiiBE (2026-09); YouTube/Chistepper.com (1994 footage); YouTube (2001 footage)

claims.claim: Mary Harris, known as 'Black Mary,' a West Side native, put on steppin' events for 62 years starting at age 17; her first event was at the Red Top on Madison Street off Pulaski (50-cent tickets, ~300 index-card handbills); she hosted parties at the Local 399 union hall for 14 years; she encountered the Jackson Five, Jerry Butler, Curtis Mayfield, the Dells and the Four Tops through the scene.
claims.evidence: Direct quoted recollections attributed to Harris; no independent corroboration found in this pass.
claims.notes: Harris is the key 'ordinary person' and woman in this brief's People section. Flagged as the most urgent oral-history capture target: her account is the only documentation of the Red Top / Local 399 venue lineage.
claims.source: YouTube: 'The History of the Chicago Dance Style Known as Steppin' From the 1940s to Today' (practitioner quotes)

claims.claim: WVAZ (102.7 FM) began Saturday-night steppers music programming in 1989, giving Chicago-style stepping a commercial-radio foothold.
claims.evidence: Single uncited source; no corroboration found.
claims.notes: Unresolved vs. the yolosteppers variant (WBMX 102.7/1390AM in the mid-to-late 1970s for Jeffree cuts). Frequency history of 102.7 (WBMX → WVAZ) needs a station-history source.
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_stepping

claims.claim: College radio station WKKC-FM 89.3 began programming steppers music in 1975, before commercial radio's interest.
claims.evidence: Single uncited claim repeated across two tertiary pages.
claims.notes: No station records, schedules, or oral histories confirming this were found. High-value archival target (Kennedy-King College archives).
claims.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_stepping; pancocojams excerpt (same text)

claims.claim: Steppers' sets are organized social events ('stepper's sets') typically catering to an older, intergenerational crowd; dress is formal ('dressed to the nines'); fashion is treated as part of the performance; the music flows between classic and neo-soul.
claims.evidence: Lixenberg/FT: 'the whole scene was thrilling: great music and people were dressed to the nines'; Fab 5 Freddy in Vibe: 'dreamlike, transcendental, rhythmic elegance.' TRiiBE: 'fashion as sharp as the footwork.' Tucker: intergenerational, socio-economically diverse group of primarily African Americans; music between classic and neo-soul.
claims.notes: This cluster is the strongest evidence for the 'community' half of the research question.
claims.source: ourdjtalk.com; Financial Times photography special (Dana Lixenberg, 2002 V103 Steppers Ball); TRiiBE (2026-09); Emory News (Tucker)
claims.source_type: community / international press / local journalism / institutional

claims.claim: The dance's basic form is a 6-count pattern danced in a lane/slot, at tempos of roughly 70–100 BPM; the leader traditionally starts on the left foot, the follower's footwork being opposite.
claims.evidence: Community-held technical description; consistent across two sources but both are non-authoritative.
claims.notes: SUPPORTED as community technical knowledge; flag that no authoritative syllabus exists to verify against (see C002).
claims.source: alchetron.com/Chicago-stepping; pancocojams (community)

claims.claim: The National Steppers Society is an organization representing steppers; per Medill (2016), the dance's roots 'come from the Bop, according to the National Steppers Society.'
claims.evidence: Single mention; no institutional records consulted.
claims.notes: Existence of the organization is PROVISIONAL until its own materials are consulted.
claims.source: Medill Reports Chicago (2016-03-03)

claims.claim: Anjulet Tucker, cultural sociologist (Emory), studied Chicago steppers in Atlanta: the dance attracts an intergenerational, socio-economically diverse group of primarily African Americans; some steppers describe connections between the dance and spirituality; the film 'Let's Get to Work: Chicago Steppin in Atlanta' (ECDS, with Clint Fluker) and the 2017-02-23 Emory program documented the Atlanta outpost.
claims.evidence: Emory's own reporting on Tucker's grant-funded study and the Rose Library event; Atlanta Studies post includes Tucker's methodological reflections on representation, authority, and preservation.
claims.notes: The only scholarly/sociological source in this brief. Tucker's planned Southern Spaces article is a follow-up target.
claims.source: Emory News (2017-02); Atlanta Studies blog (2017-04-25); ECDS/Emory Center for Digital Scholarship
claims.source_type: institutional journalism / scholarly blog / university archive

claims.claim: Good Deeds International (Atlanta) hosts an annual Heritage Ball attracting thousands of steppers from around the country; Class Act Steppers was one of the first Atlanta steppin' clubs.
claims.evidence: Tucker: 'Atlanta's pre-eminent steppers organization, Good Deeds International, will be hosting their annual Heritage Ball. It attracts thousands of Steppers from around the country.' Kharen Fulton of Class Act Steppers (d. 2016) named.
claims.notes: Second-source confirmation (event listings) would strengthen; ilovesteppin.com listings show Good Deeds International active in 2026.
claims.source: Emory News (2017-02, Tucker interview)

claims.claim: Chicago steppin' has been transplanted from Chicago to cities around the country over the past two decades; documented outposts include Atlanta, Detroit, Houston, Los Angeles, New York City, Milwaukee, Cleveland, Dallas, Baton Rouge, Baltimore/Washington DC, and Texas cities.
claims.evidence: TRiiBE lists WLSC prelim cities (Atlanta, Detroit, Houston, Los Angeles, New York City). Tucker documents Atlanta. Event listings show active sets in Gary IN, Dallas, Milwaukee, Cleveland, Baton Rouge, Norfolk, Columbus, etc.
claims.notes: Regional variant names (Detroit Ballroom, Texas Swing Out, DC Hand Dance) are community taxonomy (ourdjtalk/pancocojams) — SUPPORTED as taxonomy, not as historical claims.
claims.source: TRiiBE (2026-09); Emory/Atlanta Studies (2017); ilovesteppin.com event listings (2025–26); LSU Reveille (Baton Rouge classes)
claims.source_type: local journalism / institutional / community listings / student journalism

claims.claim: The V103 Steppers Ball at the Hyatt Regency hotel (2002) was Chicago's biggest steppin' event, documented by photographer Dana Lixenberg and Fab 5 Freddy for Vibe magazine.
claims.evidence: Lixenberg's first-person account of the commission; FT published the images with captions 'V103 Steppers Ball at the Hyatt Regency Hotel, Chicago 2002.'
claims.notes: 'Biggest' is Lixenberg's characterization — attribute. The Lixenberg images themselves are rights-held by the artist/gallery; listed as unavailable for reuse (see visuals.md).
claims.source: Financial Times photography special (Grimm gallery PDF), Lixenberg account

claims.claim: Chicagoans dance steppin' at the Richard J. Daley Center during lunch hours as exercise/stress relief.
claims.evidence: Reported with on-site photography.
claims.notes: Useful evidence of the dance's presence in civic/public space.
claims.source: Medill Reports Chicago (2016-03-03), with photo by Adriana Fernandez

claims.claim: In the steppers scene, 'experience and skill are the highest form of currency'; status terms include 'heavy hitter' for extraordinarily gifted dancers.
claims.evidence: Tucker's fieldwork-based account of community norms and her own position as a non-Chicago, non-heavy-hitter narrator.
claims.notes: Supports the analysis of hierarchy/status within the community half of the research question.
claims.source: Atlanta Studies (2017-04-25, Tucker)

claims.claim: Samantha Chatman — daughter of DJ Sam Chatman — is an Emmy Award-winning journalist at ABC7 Chicago (WLS-TV) who has reported on her father's stepping legacy.
claims.evidence: N'DIGO: 'Her father DJ Sam Chatman is known as the 'Godfather of Steppin' in Chicago.' Bronzeville Winery: Sept 25, 2023 event hosted by his daughter Samantha Chatman, Emmy-winning journalist and ABC7 anchor/reporter.
claims.notes: A rare documented woman in the stepping archive — as journalist and intergenerational transmitter.
claims.source: N'DIGO (2025-08-25); Bronzeville Winery event page (2023); WLS-TV (2022-02-09 segment cited by Wikipedia)
claims.source_type: Black press / venue page / local TV

claims.claim: The dance must not be confused with the percussive 'stepping' of Black Greek-letter organizations (NPHC); Chicago steppin' is a swing-family partner dance.
claims.evidence: Community source explicitly distinguishes the two forms.
claims.notes: Essential definitional scope for the brief (search engines and AI summaries routinely conflate them).
claims.source: Society of Boppers page (via pancocojams)

claims.claim: Steppers sets in Chicago occur 'seven days a week, almost 24 hours a day'; Chicago is 'the mecca' of the danceform.
claims.evidence: Practitioner self-description; not an independent count.
claims.notes: 'Mecca' and '24 hours' are community rhetoric; the verifiable core is that sets/classes run across the week. Debonair Steppers & Walkers 2026 day-party schedule (3rd Saturdays, Grand Ballroom, 6351 S. Cottage Grove) corroborates regular cadence.
claims.source: TRiiBE (2026-09), quoting media representative Valerie Hill

claims.claim: Stepping 'took shape in Chicago on the South and West sides during the 1940s and 1950s.'
claims.evidence: Single-source periodization; consistent with community accounts of bop-era ballrooms and clubs.
claims.notes: No archival (Defender listings, club ads) corroboration found in this pass — a primary-source gap flagged for further research.
claims.source: The TRiiBE (2026-09)

claims.claim: A weekly/monthly 'stepper's set' circuit persists in 2026: e.g., Debonair Steppers & Walkers 'Ultimate Day Party' (3rd Saturdays, Grand Ballroom, 6351 S. Cottage Grove Ave., DJ Slique Riq, $15 advance/$25 door); Sam Chatman's Capricorns Ball; Chicago Female Promoters' Harlem Nights Steppers Ball; Kevin Nevels Superbowl Extravaganza; Shawn Hayes 'Indiana's Largest Steppin' Contest' (Gary, IN).
claims.evidence: Public listings with dates, venues, DJs, ticket prices — event-level facts.
claims.notes: Listings are self-published; treat as evidence of circuit activity, not audited attendance.
claims.source: ilovesteppin.com 2025–26 event listings; YouTube promo descriptions

claims.claim: Chicago's stepper scene gave outsize local longevity to certain records: Stevie Wonder's 'Hey Love,' Gladys Knight & the Pips' 'Everybody Needs Love,' and Martha & the Vandellas' 'My Baby Loves Me' all chart higher on Chicago classic-soul countdowns than their national profiles would predict, because of steppers sets.
claims.evidence: Trade-press analysis of a 1995 classic-soul countdown: 'there's a lot of 'only in Chicago'' — attributed explicitly to 'steppers sets.'
claims.notes: Single-source but from a trade publication with domain expertise; supports the music↔community feedback-loop analysis.
claims.source: RadioInsight (Sean Ross, trade press)

claims.claim: The Society of Boppers, Steppers & Walkers (profmilesproduction.com) holds a community taxonomy: Bopping (parents of Baby Boomers; 'secret society' of social partner dancers; learned from parents/family), Walking (early 1960s; 'the black version of the waltz'; single step/double step/stride/skip walk), Steppin' (mid-1970s youth creation via the New Bop).
claims.evidence: Community-authored history page; no named author or publication date.
claims.notes: Useful as community-held terminology; 'secret society' characterization is the community's own framing — attribute, do not adopt as objective fact.
claims.source: pancocojams (quoting profmilesproduction.com)

claims.claim: The steppers' canon spans 'original cuts' (J.B.'s, Jeffree) through contemporary mainstream R&B and neo-soul (Beyoncé, Mary J. Blige, Raheem DeVaughn, Will Downing, Anthony Hamilton, Ledisi).
claims.evidence: Convergent community and scholarly accounts of a living, updating canon.
claims.notes: Supports the music-half of the research question: the canon is curated by DJs and dancers, not by the industry.
claims.source: yolosteppers.com; Emory News (Tucker: 'music that flows between classic and neo-soul')

claims.claim: Practitioner Andre 'Dre' Blackwell is a master instructor and popular influencer in the stepping community (hosted the WLSC 2026 pre-party).
claims.evidence: Single mention.
claims.notes: Named entity for the graph; no further verification.
claims.source: The TRiiBE (2026-09)

claims.claim: Local Chicago DJ Herb Kent hosted an event known as the 'World's Largest Steppers Contest' (referenced in community accounts of the Love Jones steppers scene).
claims.contradictory_evidence: TRiiBE (2026) documents Pete Frazier/Majestic Gents as longtime host/producer, with no mention of Kent.
claims.evidence: Single community source: Love Jones 'depicts an event formerly hosted by local Chicago DJ Herb Kent, known as the World's Largest Steppers Contest.'
claims.notes: The claim may conflate Herb Kent's steppers-set hosting with the WLSC. Do not publish without a second source. Herb Kent's radio legacy (WVON/WVAZ, 'The Cool Gent') is documented in BMI-002-adjacent Chicago radio history.
claims.source: ourdjtalk.com community thread

claims.claim: No named women appear in standard Chicago soul session histories (MUSIC-001); in stepping, women like Mary Harris (promoter), Samantha Chatman (journalist), Anjulet Tucker (scholar), Valerie Hill (media rep), Sherry Gordon and April 'Cincinnati Red' Burns (dancers), and the Chicago Female Promoters collective hold documented roles — but no institutional archive centers them.
claims.evidence: Synthesis: named women appear in this brief's source base, but only in practitioner quotes, event listings, and one scholar's work — not in institutional archives or published histories.
claims.notes: A finding about the archive itself, not just the dance. Kept as VERIFIED because the absence is corroborated across all consulted sources.
claims.source: CTL-DR-MUSIC-001 (gap #5); this brief's sources (TRiiBE, N'DIGO, Emory, ilovesteppin.com, practitioner interviews)
claims.source_type: sibling research / local journalism / institutional / community

grading_rubric.DISPUTED: Sources contradict each other; both positions recorded
grading_rubric.PROVISIONAL: Single source only (practitioner testimony, community site, tertiary aggregator) — not yet independently corroborated
grading_rubric.SUPPORTED: Corroborated by at least two sources, or one reputable source plus consistent practitioner testimony
grading_rubric.UNRESOLVED: No usable source found; recorded as an explicit gap
grading_rubric.VERIFIED: Corroborated by primary sources or multiple independent secondary sources of distinct provenance

title: The Chicago Steppers Ecosystem — Claim Ledger
unresolved: U01: Exact founding year and founder of the World's Largest Steppers Contest (Rodney Burke claim vs. Pete Frazier/Majestic Gents history; 35th annual in 2026 implies ~1991).
U02: WKKC-FM 89.3 steppers programming from 1975 — no station records consulted.
U03: WVAZ 102.7 Saturday-night steppers programming from 1989 — single uncited tertiary source; frequency/station-call history unreconciled with WBMX-era claims.
U04: Any primary documentation (flyer, ad, recording) of Sam Chatman's 'steppin'' coining or of 1960s–70s steppers sets in the Chicago Defender or club ephemera.
U05: Oral histories of Mary Harris ('Black Mary') beyond the single video-description account; dates of birth/death unknown.
U06: Club workers (doormen, bartenders, security, sound techs) at steppers sets — entirely unnamed in all consulted sources.
U07: Economic scale of the steppers circuit (ticket prices, promoter revenues, DJ fees) — only isolated ticket prices ($0.50 at the Red Top, 1960s; $15/$25 in 2026) documented.
U08: The planned Southern Spaces article by Anjulet Tucker — cited as 'working on' in 2017; publication status unknown.
